Donnel Stern  

THE SCOPE AND SWEEP OF PROFESSOR KUHN'S presentation are awesome. He moves from art and literature, to philosophy, to psychoanalysis, and back again, integrating as he goes, and he does so with a sure touch. He makes convincing use of his wide scholarship to establish, under the strictures of what is after all a very brief format, a vast hypothesis about the relationship of art to itself and to the person viewing or reading it.

The paper is a rescue effort. We must ruefully admit that art historians and students of literature have had some good reasons, at least until recently, not to take psychoanalysis seriously as a tool of investigation. We owe Professor Kuhns a debt of gratitude for contributing to making psychoanalysis a potentially productive member of the interpretive fields which, together, offer us a picture of the life of our culture and those which have gone before. While I do wish to begin, then, by thanking Professor Kuhns for his paper and for the opportunity to participate with him in this program, he deserves our greater appreciation for being able and willing to see beyond the received view of academia, no matter how justified it may have been in the past, and for making a new beginning, looking deeply into the crosscurrents of psychoanalysis, philosophy, and art.

Even if Professor Kuhns had not just accepted the received view, but had made his own judgment of the potential of psychoanalysis to contribute to the understanding of art, art history, and literature, he might very well have based this judgment on past efforts in this direction. If he had seen no farther than this, I think he would not have taken up the challenge which his paper represents. Too many psychoanalytic interpretations in the past were primarily a series of links, sometimes forced and often strained, between the the artist's work and the exigencies of the artist's life.

It is perhaps supportable to believe that one can look at a work of art, or read a piece of literature, and extrapolate the unconscious themes of the artist's life.

Herbert Zucker Ph.D.

Herbert Zucker

Herbert Zucker, Ph.D.
NEW YORK, NEW YORK

Herbert Zucker  

To the Editor:

IN DISCUSSING METHODS OF INQUIRY Lewis Aron (1993, p. 302) refers to a clinical example that is used in my book (1967, p. 42) to illustrate how patient summaries and conceptions of events diminish the patient's experience of such events. I also suggested that certain typically asked questions would likely further raise the level of abstraction of patient reports, while inquiries directed toward fleshing out the concrete content in the report might enhance the possibility of an experience of self in the event.

Dr. Aron, however, sees me encouraging therapists to ask "any or all" of a series of questions, including those I believe would result in cognitive condensations. Dissimilar questions, in effect dissimilar procedures, can not be placed in the same basket for they issue from different methodologies of inquiry. Different questions activate the person in varying ways, thereby determining the character of the data produced. And it is the character of the data produced that enriches or impairs experience.

To the Editor:

I HAVE ALWAYS been impressed by the originality, creativity and scholorship of papers published in Contemporary Psychoanalysis. It was with increasing dismay that I read the paper "The Opposing Currents Technique" by Steven Stern in the October, 1992 issue.

Although the author mentions a footnote that the ideas were presented in a chapter, he does not cite the book. I found that the paper in Contemporary was essentially expanded and slightly reworked version of the earlier chapter, "Managing opposing currents: An intrerpersonal psychoanalystic technique for the treating of eating disorders" in Psychodynamic Treatment of Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia edited by Craig Johnson, Ph.D. and published in 1990.

The presentation of the idea of "opposing currents", the account of Case L., the discussion, conclusion and references are almost identical to the chapter. The introduction and discussion of self-problems, some object-relations points of view and transferencce in the Contemporary paper are new. While the idea of "opposing currents" and the overarching intepersonal point of view is a welcome contribution to the literature of eating disorders, the paper in the Contemporary is not a "new" paper.

Richard Kuhns Ph.D.

Richard Kuhns

Richard Kuhns, Ph.D.
Department of Philosophy Columbia University
New York, New York 10027

Richard Kuhns  

A NATURAL CONNECTION BETWEEN HISTORY AND PSYCHOANALYSIS would seem to stem from several sources: the emphasis on the early childhood of the individual, the assumption that every symptom has a history, and the high value placed on art and culture. Moreover, psychoanalytic thought has, from its beginning, looked to the past for examples and inspiration—to ancient Greek, to Elizabethan, and to Romantic works of art. And yet with all its dedication to the past, psychoanalytic theory has seemed surprisingly and paradoxically ahistorical. By that I mean, the inquiries of art historical scholarship and literary history, are more often than not ignored or neglected in psychoanalytic interpretations of art and of artists. Rather, the early psychoanalytic interpretations concentrated on persons, the psychobiography of the artist, the approach of pathography, neglecting the larger historical context within which the artist lived and worked; an approach we might characterize as names without history—as contrasted with the opposite pole—history without names. And yet, the founders of psychoanalysis, and the psychoanalytic theory of art—Freud himself, Ernest Jones, Otto Rank—were hardly ignorant of history, and were steeped in the cultural tradition in which they were writing. So one might have supposed that they could readily have added the dimension of historical context to their interpretations.

IT'S BEEN A GREAT PLEASURE for me to meet Dr. Holland in person this evening—and a relief. I'd been half convinced he was really a conglomerate, a major industry. It's not just that he is immensely productive, but he covers so much intellectual ground in each one of his books. His curiosity, energy and grasp of so many fields is astonishing.

Dr. Holland, tonight, is showing us only the tip of his iceberg. His ambitious project is to conceptualize how texts give rise to meanings—and he has omitted, understandably, in this brief presentation what he has put together from his vast readings in linguistics, philosophy, literary theory, and neurophysiology: his ideas towards a theory of reading.

What he's done in this experiment is use the general psychoanalytic principal that our psychic life is more coherent and connected than appears. Specifically, he connects character (or identity) and linguistic behavior (or meaning). He explores the reader's "countertransference" to the poem, as he puts it. In another analogy that occurs to me, the poem becomes a kind of collective dream put into the minds of its readers who then associate to it, finding its meaning, in their own terms. We, studying this process over his shoulder, so to speak, are enriched not only because the associative/interpretive process in ourselves is aroused but also because new trains of meaning are set in motion.

I see my job this evening to help build from us to him, matching the bridge he speaks of building himself, to welcome him into our Interpersonal Institute by enlarging even further the scope of his inquiry and enterprise. Specifically, I want to get us going on his project by making some specific suggestions about what an interpersonal reading of this poem might open up for further thought and stimulation.

Let me start with some speculations about what I think might be going on in the very process of inquiry he presents to us with his students.

He rode directly into the hall, and was a man of gigantic stature; his armor and horse, his face and weapon, were green, and what he carried was not a sword but an archaic battle-ax. THE AUTHOR HAD NOT HAD CONTACT with writings about King Arthur's court and ideas of chivalry and the Troubadours since college days. Her fancied recall was that chivalry had to do with moral and ethical judgments of that time. Not so, and the brief review of the setting of the Arthurian legends (which were written in poetry, as were all recorded works of the time), perhaps indicates why this was not so. But these tales of the fantastic, mythic, and preternatural did give indication of the chivalric code: courage, devotion to liege, and acceptance of chivalric rules. Whether they had anything to do with 'romance' as we know it now, or worshipful respect of women, can perhaps be inferred from an examination of the tale of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.

Twisting Gawain's Tale

Alan Grey Ph.D.

Alan Grey

Alan Grey, Ph.D.
103 East 86th Street
New York, New York 10028

Alan Grey  

FABLES LIKE THE MILLENNARIAN legends of the Round Table carry the promise of timeless, albeit enigmatic wisdom. The self-same plots echo repeatedly through myths cherished the world over, hinting at themes deeply rooted in human nature itself, if only the hidden key were deciphered. Buried in the parable of Gawain's encounter with the Green Knight may be a clue to the nature of masculine self-realization. Typically, messages of this sort are decoded with the help of an archetype like the Oedipus complex, much consulted by analysts. The term "complex" is employed here as a reminder that Freud's exegesis, rather than the original source itself, has become the clinical paradigm. The Freudian template is bypassed here because it deals with inevitable defeat, a scenario irrelevant to Gawain's triumph.

For a plot about victory, Campbell's hero myth (1949) offers the best documented paradigm. He distilled his prototype from an extensive cross-cultural survey of religious and secular legends. Its outline is consistent with earlier and similar projects by Toynbee (1947), and by Kluckhohn (1959), and also reminiscent of Sullivan's interpersonal treatment plan (Grey, 1975).

THE HISTORY OF MODERN DYNAMIC psychotherapy has been characterized by an unceasing evolution in the language of theory and technique. One of the sub-texts of this history is the story of how particular therapists working with particular patients came to creative understandings that have become the texts of our field. Some of these pivotal patients are themselves part of the story of psychotherapy; none more so than Freud's patients. Anna O. and Dora have become objects of scholarly interest almost unto themselves. More recently, Kohut (1979) has described the paradigmatic change in his work in his two analyses of Mr. Z. from a classical analytic to a self psychological point of view. Semrad said that the patient was the only text a young therapist needed to read (Rako & Mazer, 1979). It is the thesis of this paper that, on a significantly less epoch-making level, every therapist has patients who come to be the reference points in their development as clinicians. It is these patients that one may experience as particularly "special" because the work with them is incorporated within and facilitates changes in the therapist's representational model of psychotherapy.

This incorporative dynamic within the therapist may be understood as similar to that characterized by Bowlby (1969) in his discussion of "internal working models, " or mental representations, of attachment. Such models are further defined by Main, Kaplan and Cassidy (1985) as "a set of conscious and/or unconscious rules for the organization of information relevant to attachment and for obtaining or limiting access to that information" (pp. 66–67). Dr. Stern replies:

MS. ORTMEYER'S CHARGE that I essentially recycled an earlier chapter with only minor modifications is a serious one; thus I appreciate this opportunity to respond.

I was obviously aware of the points of overlap between my earlier chapter and the Contemporary Psychoanalysis article. I therefore made reference to the former publication immediately, in the first footnote. I am confused by Ms. Ortmeyer's statement that I do "not cite the book" containing the earlier chapter. The book is listed in the reference section, but (due to a proofreading oversight on my part) under the title and expected publication date that were current at the time I first submitted the paper to Contemporary Psychoanalysis. (I note that Ms. Ortmeyer also cites the date incorrectly in her letter.) If she meant that I should have named the chapter and book in the footnote itself, I tend to agree. However, it was not my intention to downplay the relationship between the two pieces.

I disagree with Ms. Ortmeyer's characterization of the Contemporary paper as "slightly reworked." While the basic concept of "opposing currents" and the clinical case material illustrating it are indeed (for the most part) the same, the theoretical framework for understanding the technique's efficacy (constituting 12 of the paper's 19 pages of text) is almost entirely new. The earlier chapter was primarily clinical, written for an audience with a specialized interest in the psychodynamic treatment of eating disorders. The application of the opposing currents idea to work with eating disordered patients was original in that paper, but the theoretical section was brief and, from my current perspective, somewhat "primitive." The second paper was written in consequence of my more recent immersion in a variety of psychoanalytic ideas and represents a significant evolution in my thinking. It also aims to connect the opposing currents approach with certain theoretical issues and controversies in the analytic literature, and make a contribution to those debates. Contrary to Ms. Ortmeyer's suggestion, I believe this new scholarship is reflected in the reference list of the second paper, which contains 33 entries compared to 18 in the first chapter. In fact, only 14 of the original references are cited in the second paper.

Erich Fromm, The Art of Being. Foreword by Rainer Funk, 144 pages, hardcover, index, $16.95. New York: The Continuum Publishing Co.

Erich Fromm, The Revision of Psychoanalysis. Hardcover, $28.95. Boulder, CO.: Westview Press. Edited by Rainer Funk.

ERICH FROMM WAS BORN AT THE BEGINNING of the 20th Century and died eight decades later. The William Alanson White Institute—of which he was a co-founder—honored him in a memorial issue of Contemporary Psychoanalysis (Vol. 17, October, 1981). Included in the memorial publication was a dedication, tributes and commentaries, in which he was praised for his indomitable humanism and his faith in man's inherent capability of self-determination. Reference was also made to his eloquence as a speaker, teacher and writer, his quest for reason, and his love and dedication to life. At the same time, questions were raised about his not formally addressing himself to particular clinical issues, the technical aspects of treatment and case presentations. Fromm's books for the most part have avoided routine technical analytic concerns.

For the record, Fromm had been a member of the Berlin Psychoanalytic Society and was trained there. For the first ten years of his professional life he had been an orthodox Freudian analyst. As he matured professionally, he modified his views, but he was never happy with any particular label.

The Art of Being along with the powerful Revision of Psychoanalysis were posthumously published in the United States in 1992. All the material has been selected and thoughtfully edited by Rainer Funk.

Dr. Aron replies:

I APPRECIATE DR. ZUCKER'S ATTENTION to my article as well as his efforts to clarify any misunderstandings regarding his position on the methodology of psychoanalytic inquiry. My thanks as well to the editors of Contemporary Psychoanalysis for permitting me to respond to Dr. Zucker's letter. It is precisely because Dr. Zucker has made significant contributions to explicating the principles of interpersonal interviewing that I used the illustration drawn from his book and highlighted his approach to psychoanalytic inquiry.

Dr. Zucker, however, indicates that I see him as encouraging therapists to ask "any and all" of a series of questions, including some questions that he believes do not fit his recommendations and would therefore elicit a character of data different from that which would be produced by his own methodology.

In my article, I did not suggest that "any and all" questions would be recommended by Dr. Zucker, but rather that he might ask "any and all of the following questions " (emphasis added, p. 302). The following questions consisted of a series of seven questions. "Are you this way in other situations? When did you first notice this sort of thing? What other things were you thinking about? What was being talked about? Who did the 'we' refer to? Who was actually there? What did you actually say?" (p. 302). Each of these questions, in my view, was directed specifically at getting the kind of data that Dr. Zucker is interested in, namely, at "fleshing out the concrete details of the report" and acquiring the "particulars concerning where, when, and what" (p. 42). The questions were designed to fulfill Dr. Zucker's stated goals, namely that "Events need to be recreated in such a way that it is almost possible to visualize the scene and hear the actors" (p. 42).

Now, of course, Dr. Zucker and I might disagree about whether or not a particular question or phrasing would be likely to raise the level of abstraction of patient reports or alternatively help to flesh out the concrete content of the report. However, what is most puzzling, is that it was not I who suggested these questions but rather Dr. Zucker himself. Every one of these questions was suggested by Dr. Zucker in his original description of the case (p. 43).

I

ANY WORK OF ART CAN BE VIEWED not only as an expression of the genius of its creator but also as representative of the spirit of its time. Each society, in its literature, its paintings, its rituals, recreates and retells its myths, those central thematic threads which ultimately shape the world view and experience of its members. Its heroes express its hopes, ideals and conflicts; the hero's acts become reaffirmations of the principles guiding the culture and the retelling serves to inculcate more firmly the society's values and beliefs. For these reasons, the narrative content and the symbolism of a work of literature must be viewed through the eyes of the people who lived at the time of its authorship; it is in this way that the current reader may more fully realize the concerns, intellectual and spiritual, which manifest themselves in the work and make it of a piece with its own time.

The author of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight is unknown but is believed to have been a member of the aristocracy living in England in the Fourteenth Century. As a Romance of the late Medieval period, the story utilizes common themes found in contemporaneous and earlier works: knights are bold, challenges are made, contests take place and acts of chivalry are displayed. Indeed, the work can be read and enjoyed just simply on that level, as a good yarn about Round Table characters, an adventure story containing elements of farce, suspense and daring. What makes it more than that, however, is that it captures in its story and Gawain's trials aspects fundamental to Medieval man's vision of his world and his existence.

What can be said, briefly, which describes the spirit of this time so removed from our own?

Is there a Psychologically Real?

Leston Havens M.D.

Leston Havens

Leston Havens, M.D.
151 Brattle Street
Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138

Leston Havens  

I ASK THIS QUESTION aware that the "psychologically real" is a deliberate oxymoron. The psychological refers to how we see things, our outlooks or perspectives, while the real refers to what is beyond any particular perspective, if only because no perspective can include everything. The artist Magritte called attention to the difference: this is not a pipe but a picture of a pipe. On the other hand, Cezanne implied he did not want to paint pictures but to be like nature and make apples; why not, he said, since he was part of nature? The problem is also a clinical one if we do not want to give accounts of patients, describing how they conform to this or that idea, but to reach the patients themselves.

The problem gains immediacy when the patient does not "seem real." Imposters and "as if" personalities refer to the most discussed examples of this possibility; yet among "false personalities, " to use Winnicott's term, appear the commonest instances. As soon as the idea of psychological disguises or character armor gains currency and with it the idea of a truer part, the psychologically real presents as a problem in recognition and recovery.

It presents theoretically in such ideas as "being true to oneself." The self has an ambiguous status in psychoanalytic theory, sometimes being merely a fantasy of the ego, so that "true to oneself" means being true to a fantasy. Or the self may refer to a supraordinate structure so that being true to this larger self carries greater weight. I have argued elsewhere (Havens, 1986) that the ego finds its self in the superego and ego ideal, that is, in the values, aspirations, and prohibitions it makes its own, with the result, a self to which one is true or not. In reply it can be said these are merely fantasies of the good or bad to which we may or may not adhere. For myself, I find this language inadequate to the problem of psychological ownership, the experience of going from an ego which mediates among forces to a self which is defined by its taking responsibility for particular psychological decisions as its own.

To the Editor:

THE AWARENESS OF THE LOOSE CONNECTION between psychoanalytic theory and practice is an old one although it continues to receive too little attention. Many others and I have been interested in this issue for some time (Witenberg, 1976), (1978), (1987) ; (Berger, 1985). George Klein's question, "Two Theories or One?" (1973), the eponymous title of his well-known essay, brought the matter in sharp focus as did Louis Berger in his thoroughly researched treatise Psychoanalytic Theory and Clinical Relevance(1985). In my address "Clinical Innovations and Theoretical Controversy, " (1987), I inadvertently failed to list Dr. Berger's book (1985). This important contribution should have been noted and I do so now to set the record straight. Berger's scholarly work was especially useful, not only as an important source of quotations but for its thorough discussion of the problem. Indeed, particularly in the introductory section of my article, I relied on Berger's scholarly and thoughtful summary of the thorny philosophical issues regarding the logical necessity to tie psychoanalytic theory to practice. Berger underscores the observation made by many of us, that innovations in psychoanalytic theorizing, despite their evident clarification of language and concepts, have not led to improvement in therapeutic efficacy. The logical connection between the two leaves a lot to be desired.

It could be that Freud (1910) and the rest of us have been asking the wrong question.

DURING THOSE FIRST SESSIONS OF SUPERVISION with Erich Fromm, I began to wonder if I might do better as a necktie salesman. Because my color sense is unreliable, there was no recourse but to persevere at clinical endeavors. The source of my despair was confusion evoked by Fromm's assessment of the case under consideration. As I perceived the patient, a journalist, he was compulsive, acerbic, and unremittingly dissatisfied with everything—his marriage, his parents, his boss, and most certainly his treatment results. That characterization brought an impatient response from Fromm. "Isn't it obvious?", he insisted, "He regards himself as a package, a commodity. He wraps himself attractively to induce a sale. But he offers no inner substance. Characterologically, he has a typical marketing orientation."

To picture this bitter and cynical patient as trying to recommend himself to me was absolutely bewildering. His every communication echoed with disparagement of my professional contribution or of my person. On the other hand, it was impossible to dismiss a firm opinion offered by Fromm, whose ideas were opening new vistas in psychoanalysis. After a few more sessions of existential turmoil for me, somehow we shifted to another case. It may have been a deliberate mutual decision. In any event, subsequent meetings came closer to my initial hopes for understandable challenges. No longer was there cause to agonize over an impasse so foreign to my comprehension as to shake trust in my own immediate experience.

Looking back brings with it a question about what deterred my customary argumentativeness in defense of my own views. In answer, Fromm's image rises once again to my mind's eye.

SIR GAWAIN AND THE GREEN KNIGHT from Four Romances from the Cycle of King Arthur reprinted in this issue of Contemporary Psychoanalysis is a fascinating tale filled with themes and symbolism well suited to consideration in our present life and has much in it that can be applied to psychoanalysis. There are issues of loyalty, authority, sex, death, fear, and relationships between people, to name a few. The search of Gawain can in itself be considered as a metaphor for the process of psychoanalysis.

In this story, after having rejected the temptations offered by the seductive wife of the Green Knight, Sir Gawain finally accepts the green girdle, "a bit of green lace" as a protective amulet1 against unknown fate. In the end he is rewarded for having refused the sexual temptations proffered by the wife of the Green Knight (at the direction of her husband), but is punished with a scratch for having accepted the lace and failing to report it. What are we to make of this? Is the author a creative artist who communicates through his writing a message of which he himself may or may not be aware, and that in some way touches the unconscious of the readers and the conscious analytic mind of the psychoanalyst? If so, what is that message?

The liars showed courage and resolution in their opposition to the scientists who with their pernicious doctrines bid fair to strip every shred of self-deception from their dupes leaving them without any of the natural protection necessary for the preservation of their mental health against the impact of truth. Some, knowing full well the risks that they ran, nevertheless laid down their lives in affirmation of lies so that the weak and doubtful would be convinced by the ardour of their conviction of the truth of even the most preposterous statements. It is not too much to say that the human race owes its salvation to that small band of gifted liars who were prepared even in the face of indubitable facts to maintain the truth of their falsehoods. Even death was denied and the most ingenious arguments were educed to support obviously ridiculous statements that the dead lived on in bliss. These martyrs to untruth were often of humble origin whose very names have perished. But for them and the witness borne by their obvious sincerity the sanity of the race must have perished under the load placed on it. By laying down their lives they carry the morals of the world on their shoulders. Their lives and the lives of their followers were devoted to the elaboration of systems of great intricacy and beauty in which the logical structure was preserved by the exercise of a powerful intellect and faultless reasoning. By contrast the feeble processes by which the scientists again and again attempted to support their hypotheses made it easy for the liars to show the hollowness of the pretensions of the upstarts and thus to delay, if not to prevent, the spread of doctrines whose effect could only have been to induce a sense of helplessness and unimportance in the liars and their beneficiaries.

IN THIS PAPER I WILL REVIEW some of the ideas of Georg Lukács, a brilliant thinker, theoretician and critic, that still have contemporary value for psychoanalysis and philosophy. This is true despite the inconsistencies, ambiguities, and many recantations in Lukács's writings. Lukács (1885–1971) is known as a major figure of western Marxism, a term coined by Merleau-Ponty to designate a philosophical position that hoped to refurbish and improve on Marx's reductionistic vision of the proletarian revolution as a historical necessity. The book that gave Lukács his reputation, History and Class Consciousness(1982), was actually repudiated by him, and the work he regarded as his greatest intellectual work, the volumes on Ontology, are almost completely unread and unreadable.

Kadarkay's recent (1991) biography of Lukács is not as good as the classic works on Lukács by Parkinson (1977) and on the young Lukács by Congdon (1983) and Gluck (1985), especially because it becomes confused on his politics and is unclear as an exposition of his thought. In a way this is forgivable, because Lukács changed his mind many times, often under the rule of political oppressors in order to save his life. Also, one of the greatest weaknesses of Lukács's thought is that he tends to politicize every issue and wrap it in Marxist jargon, which makes reading him tedious. Part of this I believe is because Lukács, perhaps like Gorbachev to whom he has been compared, was constantly torn between liberalization and holding on to absolute orthodoxy, and uncertain of where he himself stood.

FAILURES OF LOVE HAVE ALWAYS PLAYED a prominent role in prompting individuals to seek psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Contemporary theorists (e.g., Kernberg, 1974) regard the inability to fall in love as a sign of severe character pathology. Dr. Walter Spear's patient, Jack, entered therapy because he feared that he is incapable of remaining in love with and maintaining a commitment to a woman. My discussion seeks to further our understanding of this young man's perceived deficiencies in loving. I will organize the "facts" of the case to highlight issues relevant to the patient's character traits and character pathology. My working assumption is that paying closer attention to the "hysterical" aspects of Jack's style would pave the way for a constructive exploration of the core conflicts and themes that are dramatically enacted in the manifest content of the dream that is at the center of Dr. 'Spear's case report.

Problems of Differential Diagnosis

When you think of an obsessive do you tend to think of a male, just as when you think of a hysteric do you tend to think of a female? Existing theories and research support this gender bias (Warner, 1978). We have far less information regarding the manifestations of the hysterical personality disorder in men than in women (Luisada, Peele, and Pittarel 1974). Not surprisingly, a common diagnostic error is the failure to recognize the presence of hysterical trends in men. I believe that substantial hysterical trends can be discerned in the expressive, cognitive, and interpersonal aspects of Jack's style.

In comparison to the protypical male obsessional patient, Jack is not exclusively devoted to work and productivity to the exclusion of pleasure (Salzman, 1968) ; (Shapiro, 1965). His life structure is not achievement-dominated (Levenson et al., 1978). He is not driven by the wish to win respect and avoid failure at all costs. Rather, his outlook on "reality, " broadly conceived, is primarily "romantic" (Schafer, 1970).

ONE OF THE GREATEST PROBLEMS of psychoanalytic theorizing is the tendency to deal with the complexities and ambiguities of psychic life by simplifying, dichotomizing and splitting, by resorting to "either-or" instead of "both-and" solutions. One manifestation of this is the splitting of two areas of scholarship, which if studied together, could enrich each other. This has been the case in the tendency to isolate the study of the cognitive and the study of the affective. Even sophisticated psychoanalysts and cognitive theorists have made the mistake of identifying Piaget with the cognitive and psychoanalysis with the affective, and in so doing have unnecessarily and unfortunately perpetuated the splitting and isolation of these two worlds of scholarship. Often, Piaget is considered as an interesting theorist for child therapists or for cognitive theorists or for those interested in child development or structuralist philosophy, but of limited usefulness for the clinical analyst working with adults. IN CONSIDERING THE RANGE OF CONCEPTUAL and therapeutic issues that arise during the analytic treatment of a patient such as the man presented by Dr. Spear, it is worthwhile to at least acknowledge that whatever is said is inevitably played against the background of differential diagnosis and its subtle influence on what an analyst hears and what stance he takes with his patient. It is good to have on the trip but don't take the label overly seriously; just take in enough of it to keep you from feeling too empty on the journey. SANDOR FERENCZI CONTRIBUTED GREATLY to the development and spread of psychoanalysis, as well as to the germination of ideas and innovative clinical practices of his pupils and those who successively were inspired by them. Mihaly Balint, Ernest Jones (who would become his persecutor), Melanie Klein, Sandor Lorand, Sandor Rado, Geza Roheim, Clara Thompson and Imre Hermann were among Ferenczi's patients. Each of his pupils went on to make significant contributions to psychoanalysis.

To understand Ferenczi's work and personality the study of his writings between 1899 and 1908—the date he met Freud and was converted to psychoanalysis—is particularly important. These early writings were found and published for the first time in the West in 1992 (Ferenczi, 1992). They reveal Ferenczi's prevalent interests and his style, and help us better to realize this great pioneer's work.

Ferenczi's preanalytic works were gathered and nearly all published in Gyogyaszat (therapy), a progressive review edited by Miksa Schachter. Some brief fragments are also found in Orvosi Hetilap (Medical Weekly). Ferenczi had found with Schachter, his first teacher, a deep and lasting relationship, comparable in its structure to the one he had with Freud, although this relationship developed in a less conflictual way. Such a tie was personally significant considering his similar relationship with his elder brother during his childhood.

KINGS WHO WERE WONT TO KILL the bearers of ill tidings, knew something that psychoanalysts are just beginning to understand; namely, that the messenger is the message. To quote Crapanzano;

Where does the messenger stand? He himself is not without desire. He is not without power. He lives in a world charged with value, with loyalties and with animosities. … He has to understand the message, to interpret it, translate, contextualize, and elaborate it, and he has to justify all these procedures. He has responsibility! The messenger is not an automation—that fictitious role—in which he is socially cast per necessitatem(Crapanzano, 1992).

For all of Freud's devotion to the classic determinism of the Greek myths, his psychoanalysis was firmly imbedded in the rabbinic tradition; where infinity of meaning and plurality of interpretation are the cardinal virtues (Handleman, 1982, p. 21). Even now, all contemporary psychoanalytic interpretive systems offer so much latitude and choice (timing, focus, developmental level of interpretation, resistance, transference) that every interpretative offering of our messenger, the therapist, is inevitably a highly overdetermined participation which reveals as much about the therapist as it does about the patient. And, what is even more disconcerting, the patient usually knows it. It is this latter aspect of the issue—the patient's awareness of the therapist's participation—which presents us with the greatest theoretical and clinical discomfort.

DISGUST IS AMONG THE least studied of the basic emotions. This inattention may follow from something threatening about the disgust emotion. Unlike shame, another once-neglected emotion, disgust seldom causes deep pain, so qualities other than painfulness must account for its neglect. The essence of disgust is rejection of contact and the field has responded to the emotion by rejecting contact. This behavior makes sense to disgust researchers in that a basic rule of the emotion is the rule of contamination (Rozin & Fallon, 1987). Contact with the disgusting makes one disgusting. To study disgust is to risk contamination; jokes about his or her unwholesome interests soon greet the disgust researcher. One of the initial reviewers of this paper commented, "I suppose a symposium on disgust would turn me on as much as Dahlberg's book on feces. Something like approaching the unapproachable."

Disgust is unique among the emotions in its close linkage with a set of stimuli that are not interpersonal. Most of these non-human stimuli are food substances, or in some instances substances experienced by touch (e.g., slimy things). Disgust stands apart from many other emotions, which seem fundamentally interpersonal in their design. Shame and guilt are examples of profoundly interpersonal emotions that cannot be imagined apart from interpersonal life. Other emotions occupy a third position; they are responses to stimuli that can be human or non-human. Surprise is an example, as are joy and anger.

Disgust's meaning as a bad-food response is so strong for most people that they barely conceive of it outside that context.

Freud addressed the question of "Why war?" Erich Fromm studied the causes of human destructiveness. Sullivan took part in studies of how to avert further wars. THE "PAST" OF THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN psychoanalysis and literature is now nearly a hundred years old. It has been rehearsed many times, at least twice by me (1976), (1978), (and 1990). I want to shorten this survey by putting it in terms of a three-by-three-by-three matrix.

We can think of psychoanalysis as having three phases (Holland 1976), (1978). In the first phase, Freud made his great original discoveries. I mean his discoveries of free association, unconscious processes, the oedipus complex, and infantile sexuality. I would define this first phase as one in which people explained things by the relationship between conscious and unconscious.

Then came a second phase. Freud rethought the model he built on his original discoveries, and he and his colleagues in Vienna in the 1920s and '30s developed the structural id—ego—superego model, the principle of multiple function, and what we think of as ego-psychology. I would define this second phase as one in which people explained things by the relationship between the ego and the nonego, the nonego being the id, the superego, and the external world.

Near the end of his life, Husserl, Heidegger's teacher, saw the tragic irony: that the sciences our vision produced … have turned against us … separating our vision from its rootedness in our dreams, our needs and hopes; concealing from our view the depth of the field in which visible and invisible intersect and interpenetrate. THIS PAPER PLAYS OUT A NOTION of the depth of the field as it applies to the psychoanalytic situation. The field, accordingly, is the interpersonal field, all that obtains between analyst and analysand, and including the intrapersonal constellation of self each brings to the dyad. The field might be conceived of as incubator of the transference (e.g. Freud, 1940), or as transferential-countertransferential matrix (e.g. Racker, 1968), as narrative domain (e.g. Spence, 1982), or as empathic arena (e.g. Kohut, 1984). IN STRESSING FROMMIAN THEMES in this case, no claim is made to founding a Frommian school of psychoanalysis—something to which Fromm himself was much opposed. In an unpublished chapter of To Have or to Be?, Fromm (1975) wrote:

In the past I sometimes used the term "humanistic" psychoanalysis, and then dropped it, partly because it was taken over by a group of psychologists whose views I did not share, partly because I wanted to avoid the impression that I was establishing a new "school" of psychoanalysis. As far as schools of psychoanalysis are concerned, experience has shown that they are detrimental to the theoretical development of psychoanalysis and to the competence of their practitioners (pp. 95–96 of the original typescript).

It is suggested, instead, that there already exists an alternative approach to psychoanalysis, which was started by Ferenczi and then proceeded in two directions: the British "Middle Group" and the American interpersonal-cultural school. With regard to Freud's rejection of the seduction theory in 1897, this approach may be characterized as involving the reappraisal of real-life situations in parent-child relationships. It practically coincides with that group of psychoanalytic theories which Greenberg and Mitchell (1983) term "relations-oriented."

This alternative approach has already been partly shaped by Fromm. Further important contributions can come from Fromm by calling attention to neglected aspects of his published works and by drawing on his unpublished writings.

A PATIENT, A 42-YEAR-OLD PROFESSIONAL woman, moves rapidly onto the couch for her session. With an agitated tone and at a rapid pace, she describes being "upset" after the last session. She felt the analyst was being too rational, implying that she ought to accept her mother's recent death, and her analyst's impending vacation. She felt that by discussing her intensely emotional responses to these occurrences as difficulties with separation, the analyst implied that she should develop equanimity toward these life events. Since what she felt was anything but equanimity, she wondered whether she could ever improve in treatment. Perhaps she is too sick to be helped.

The analyst's theory about the role of emotions in health, in pathology, and in the treatment process is, I believe, a crucial determinant in how this clinical moment is experienced and responded to. What, for example, makes an emotional response "healthy"? Is it that the emotion expressed seems appropriate to the occasion, or that its intensity feels "right, " or that the affect facially expressed matches the affect implied by the words? However formulated or unformulated they may be, the analyst's beliefs about healthy and appropriate emotionality will influence which aspects of the patient's communication become the analytic focus of attention.

Beliefs about what constitutes "healthy" emotional responses directly shape the analyst's definition of therapeutic goals. Many analysts responding to this vignette would view as part of the therapeutic task the clarification of the patient's description of being "upset." Introduction

THEORIES OF DEVELOPMENT ARE OFTEN appealing to clinicians because they seem tidy. The epistemological premise is that development refers to events which have occurred in the past and thus its purview is defined and contained. In the psychoanalytic tradition development seems to progress linearly in sharp contrast to the zig-zagging meanderings of therapeutic process. Interpersonal analysts, for the most part, have not dutifully tended this backyard garden, but have rather moved into the thicket of transference and countertransference. Their loyalty to the idea of the interpersonal, especially their desire to describe with precision the participants of a participant-observer matrix may account for this, but reflection on the significance of developmental theory to interpersonal praxis is overdue. I believe that a consideration of developmental assumptions can contribute to our understanding of the therapeutic field.

Wrightsman (1988) has heuristically identified three categories of developmental theories: 1) early formation theories which stress the first few years of life; 2) stage theories which focus on tasks germane to each stage of development, and; 3) dialectical approaches, which chart a timeless struggle between fundamental polarities in personality structure.

Carolyn Grey  

THERE WAS A RECENT CARTOON in The New Yorker showing an obviously blue-blooded executive being interviewed on a television talk show about his successful career. Addressing the host with aristocratically locked jaw and hooded eyes, he said something like "Actually, Lou, I think it was more than being a self-made man, or being in the right place at the right time. I think it was being the right race, the right religion, the right sex, the right socioeconomic group, having the right accent, the right clothes, going to the right schools …"

Though the interviewee's comment was implausible coming from one of the elite, the cartoonist clearly understood the impact of membership in various social categories on individual identity and life experience. Psychoanalytic theorists have not always been so perceptive. However, to return to our beginnings, from its inception, psychoanalysis has implicitly concerned itself with the social roots of character. Thus it has promised a radical critique of the existing societal order. Freud himself suggested a sociallyfocused developmental theory, simultaneously initiating a tradition of cultural criticism, when he exposed the psychic damage wrought by repression and hypocrisy regarding the sexual and aggressive aspects of human nature. Further, the clinical method we inherit from him—that of inquiry and interpretation—is inherently subversive in that it potentially challenges, at the level of the individual psyche, all received meanings, including our most sacred canons.

THIS PAPER ADDRESSES THE POTENTIAL presence of therapeutic factors in a non-analytic setting. It developed partly in response to a personal experience, and out of my ongoing interest in the therapeutic function of non-interpretive aspects of psychoanalytic process. This factor, which has been variously described, refers to that dimension of psychoanalysis which involves the analyst's symbolic and actual function as a receiver of the patient's experience. In that capacity, the analyst has been said to provide or to represent an environmental mediator (Spitz, 1956), a background of safety (Sandler, 1960), an extra-uterine matrix (Mahler, 1968) or basic unit (Little, 1981), a protective shield (Khan, 1963), a holding environment (Winnicott, 1965a), (1965b), an emotional container (Bion, 1962) ; (1963) and a transformational object (Bollas, 1987). While some believe that if analysis is to produce change, this non-interpretive factor is always central, others focus on the non-interpretive holding factor in the treatment of only certain patient groups. These include patients needing a regression or suffering from a basic fault (Winnicott, 1965) ; (Balint, 1968), from narcissistic issues (Modell, 1975) ; (1976) or from severe borderline pathology (Slochower, 1992). What unifies these varied models is the critical importance given to the analyst's capacity to receive, hold, and to survive the patient's intense emotional experiences. Josephine Anderson  

ANTHROPOLOGICAL EVIDENCE SUGGESTS THAT EXCHANGE is a central feature of human existence. Exchanges may involve goods, people (as in marriage) or non-physical commodities, such as confidences and secrets. As Tiger and Fox put it: "The exchange of property (real or incorporeal) is the basic act of truly human social relationships" (1974, p. 181).

Anthropological studies show exchanges typically occurring across and between territories. In the exchange of confidences, as in intimate relationships, that which is told crosses the boundaries of different experiential zones. In this paper, we explore this phenomenon. We suggest that exchange has a developmental history which is disrupted in those with personality disorder. We present a case in which a patient's evolution towards health involved the capacity for mature exchange, manifest in a particular form of gift giving. The discussion begins with a consideration of experiential space.

Karl Jaspers wrote that "everything in the world that is presented to us comes to us in space and time and we experience it in these terms" (1962, p. 79). An awareness of its space underpins our ordinary lived experience. Despite its fundamental nature, relatively little attention has been paid to the sense of personal spatiality, at least since the era of existential psychiatry. This neglect is due, in part, to the abstract and difficult nature of the subject. The English philosopher, Gilbert Ryle, identified one of the main problems in our attempts to conceive a personal spatiality. In his influential book, The Concept of Mind, he set about exploding what he saw as myths about "the nature and place of minds" (1963, p. 13).

IN A PREVIOUS PAPER (Buchholz & Wolf, 1991) we introduced an addition to Winnicott's concept of the holding environment called the "negative holding environment." We used the term "negative" to suggest lapses in the holding environment in its traditional connotation as a facilitating process. We described a phenomenon in which issues of separation, loss and self-definition were critical to understanding both misattunements in the early environment and later treatment impasses. We defined the concept thus:

A negative holding environment protects the child from undue anxiety and provides stimulation, but does so by overly limiting the child's movements. Thus, it holds without sufficiently facilitating development. Negative holding occurs when the mother envisioned as holding the child safe is also experienced and incorporated as the critical, elusive, and hard to engage mother who may disappear if the child is not constantly vigilant and available (p. 9).

Although we described the negative holding environment as it appears in more subtle and covertly traumatizing experiences, we suggested that the concept might also be useful in understanding why abused children often cling so tenaciously to the abusive parent. Such depressed and abused children may feel that their only chance for connection is within a negatively-tinged affective experience which binds them to the parent and restricts growth.

In treatment, the holding environment has traditionally been viewed as a positive and healthy condition which facilitates growth.

AS I FIRST MET JACK in the waiting room of my office a little over a year ago, he approached me with the sort of deference usually reserved by the devout penitent for his beloved, though righteous, confessor. He sat down and avoided much eye contact but proceeded to dutifully confess the sins that had impelled him to finally arrange an appointment to enter treatment. He recently had semi-terminated a relationship of four years duration with a successful, talented and attractive young woman who loved him and wanted to get married. This wasn't the first time this had happened. Twice before he had become "frozen" as the question of commitment came up and twice before had ended "good" relationships. The same pattern permeated all corners of his life. He could not make up his mind. He could not commit himself.

Attempting to buy a new watch resulted in months of torturous ambivalence and self doubt. He could easily afford but was unable to buy a new watch. At work, he felt stuck in much the same fashion, a small cog lost in the pyramid of a mega-corporation, unable to take the risks necessary to distinguish himself though, as I later discovered, the reports of this inertness were somewhat exaggerated. It turned out he has actually had significant success at work and was one of only two people in the entire company to be sponsored for a prestigious executive degree program. Most of all, though, he feared his inability to commit himself to a relationship. He dreaded the potential of a lonely, desolate old age. This fear was what compelled him to seek treatment.
